items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: Why does a train's horn change pitch as the train rushes past a crossing?

body.html: A train horn emits a steady frequency 𝑓<sub>s</sub>. We need to explain why the horn sounds higher while the train approaches and lower after it passes.

This is the Doppler effect. The speed of sound in air depends only on the air, not on the motion of the source. When the train moves toward you, each new crest is emitted from a spot closer to you than the last one, so the crests are bunched up (shorter wavelength). Since the wave speed is the same, more crests arrive each second, so the frequency is higher.
Approaching: 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 𝑓<sub>s</sub>
<sup>𝑣</sup><sup>−</sup><sup>𝑣</sup><sub>s</sub> > 𝑓<sup>s</sup>. Receding: the source velocity points away from you, so 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 𝑓<sub>s</sub>
<sup>𝑣</sup><sup>+</sup><sup> </sup><sup>|</sup><sup> 𝑣</sup><sub>s</sub><sup>|</sup> < 𝑓<sup>s</sup>. As the train passes, the heard frequency drops from the high value to the low value.

answer.html: The train moves toward you, then away. Approaching, the sound waves are compressed (shorter 𝜆, higher 𝑓, higher pitch). Receding, they are stretched (longer 𝜆, lower 𝑓, lower pitch). The horn's own frequency never changes.

check.html: If the train is stopped (𝑣<sub>s</sub> = 0) the formula gives 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 𝑓<sub>s</sub>, so there is no shift, as expected.

items.title: CER: Make Your Claim / Explain Your Reasoning (Module 14, opener and wrap-up)

body.html: A horn of frequency 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 440 Hz on a train moving at 𝑣<sub>s</sub> = 30.0 m/s past a crossing, with 𝑣= 343 m/s. Write a claim, evidence, and reasoning for why the pitch changes.
Use the Doppler effect for a moving source and a stationary listener.
Approaching:
Receding:

Claim: The pitch changes because the train's motion changes how often sound crests reach your ear (the Doppler effect). Evidence: The 440 Hz horn is heard at about 482 Hz approaching and 405 Hz receding. The wavelength of the sound is shorter in front of a moving source and longer behind it. Reasoning: The speed of sound is fixed by the air (𝑣= 𝑓𝜆). When 𝜆 is shortened, 𝑓= 𝑣/ 𝜆 rises; when 𝜆 is lengthened, 𝑓 falls. Pitch is set by frequency, so you hear a higher pitch approaching and a lower pitch receding.

answer.html: The evidence supports the claim: relative motion of source and listener changes the frequency detected, so the pitch changes even though the horn's frequency stays at 440 Hz. (A CER is open-ended; this is a model response.)

check.html: 482 Hz and 405 Hz bracket the 440 Hz source, matching "higher, then lower."

items.title: Focus Question: What factors affect the pitch of the sound you hear from a passing motorcycle?

answer.html: Pitch depends on the frequency of the sound wave (more vibrations per second means a higher pitch). The engine sets the emitted frequency, but relative motion between the motorcycle and you changes the frequency you detect (the Doppler effect): higher while it approaches and lower while it leaves.

items.title: Get It? (page 362): Estimate the speed of sound in air at 35°C

body.html: 𝑣= 343 m/s at 20°C; speed rises about 0.6 m/s per 1°C. Find 𝑣 at 35°C.
Sound travels faster in warmer air; use the book's linear rule.
The temperature change is 35 −20 = 15°C.

check.html: Larger than 343 m/s, as expected for warmer air.

items.title: Get It? (page 364): What characteristic of a sound wave determines whether a flute note is high or low?

answer.html: Frequency. A higher frequency is heard as a higher pitch.

items.title: Get It? (page 364): How much more intense is a 90 dB sound than a 30 dB sound?

body.html: Sound levels of 90 dB and 30 dB. Find the ratio, using the book's rule that each 20 dB is a factor of 10.
The decibel scale is logarithmic. Every 20 dB is a factor of 10.
The difference is 90 −30 = 60 dB, which is three steps of 20 dB.

answer.html: 1000 times as great (in the book's pressure-amplitude convention, where 20 dB corresponds to a factor of 10).

check.html: Three 20 dB steps give three factors of 10, and a 60 dB gap is large, so a big ratio makes sense.

items.title: Figure 4 (Infer): About how many times louder does a leaf blower (90 dB) sound than a quiet conversation in a library (60 dB)?

body.html: Leaf blower 90 dB, library conversation 60 dB. Find the perceived loudness ratio.
The book states that most people perceive a 10 dB increase as about twice as loud, so each 10 dB step doubles perceived loudness.
90 −60 = 30 dB, which is three 10 dB steps, so three doublings.

answer.html: About 8 times as loud.

check.html: A 30 dB gap is a large difference, so a multiple well above 2 is reasonable.

items.title: Figure 6 (Describe): An ambulance siren emits 800 Hz and moves at 20.0 m/s along a straight road. What is the relative difference in the frequency detected by observer A, ahead of it, and observer B, behind it?

body.html: 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 800 Hz, 𝑣<sub>s</sub> = 20.0 m/s, 𝑣= 343 m/s, both observers at rest. Find 𝑓<sub>A</sub> and 𝑓<sub>B</sub> and compare them with 𝑓<sub>s</sub>.
Observer A is in front, where the waves are compressed; observer B is behind, where they are stretched. Use the Doppler formula for a moving source.

answer.html: Observer A hears about 850 Hz (about 6% above the emitted 800 Hz) and observer B hears about 756 Hz (about 5.5% below it). So 𝑓<sub>A</sub> > 𝑓<sub>s</sub> > 𝑓<sub>B</sub>, with a difference of about 94 Hz between the two.

check.html: 𝜆<sub>A</sub> is shorter and 𝜆<sub>B</sub> is longer than 𝑣/ 𝑓<sub>s</sub>, matching a higher and a lower frequency.

items.title: Get It? (page 366): Compare the wavelength and frequency heard by an observer in front of a moving train horn with those heard behind it.

body.html: A horn with 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 400 Hz moves at 30.0 m/s; 𝑣= 343 m/s. Find the wavelength and frequency in front of and behind it.

In front, the crests are emitted 𝑣<sub>s</sub> closer each period, so 𝜆<sub>front</sub> = (𝑣−𝑣<sub>s</sub>) / 𝑓<sub>s</sub>. Behind, 𝜆<sub>behind</sub> = (𝑣+ 𝑣<sub>s</sub>) / 𝑓<sub>s</sub>. The detected frequency is 𝑓= 𝑣/ 𝜆.
𝜆<sub>front</sub> = 343 −30.0

answer.html: In front: 𝜆≈0.783 m, 𝑓≈438 Hz. Behind: 𝜆≈0.933 m, 𝑓≈368 Hz. The shorter wavelength in front gives the higher frequency; 𝑓𝜆= 343 m/s in both places.

check.html: The horn's own wavelength is 343 / 400 = 0.858 m, which lies between 0.783 m and 0.933 m.

items.title: Practice Problems (Doppler effect) Problem 1 (Lesson 1, Practice Problem 1): A scooter sounds a 392 Hz horn while moving directly away from you at 18.5 m/s. What frequency do you hear? (Use 𝑣= 343 m/s.)

body.html: 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 392 Hz, 𝑣= 343 m/s, |𝑣<sub>s</sub> | = 18.5 m/s, 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = 0. Find 𝑓<sub>d</sub>.
Moving source, stationary detector. The positive direction is from the source to the detector, so a source moving away has 𝑣<sub>s</sub> = −18.5 m/s.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>d</sub> ≈372 Hz

check.html: Lower than 392 Hz, as required for a receding source.

items.title: 2 (Lesson 1, Practice Problem 2): Riding toward a siren

question.html: A motorcyclist rides at 31.0 m/s directly toward a stationary siren that emits 412 Hz. What frequency does the motorcyclist hear? (Use 𝑣= 343 m/s.)

body.html: 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = 31.0 m/s toward the siren, 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 412 Hz, 𝑣= 343 m/s, source at rest (𝑣<sub>s</sub> = 0). Find 𝑓<sub>d</sub>.
Moving detector, stationary source. The positive axis points from source to detector, but the motorcyclist moves toward the source, so 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = −31.0 m/s.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>d</sub> ≈449 Hz

check.html: Higher than 412 Hz, because the rider runs into more crests each second.

items.title: 3 (Lesson 1, Practice Problem 3): Two cars approaching each other

body.html: One car honks a 520 Hz horn while moving at 22.0 m/s toward a second car, which moves at 28.0 m/s toward the first. Find the frequency heard in the second car. ( 𝑣= 343 m/s.)

Both source and detector move. With the axis from source to detector: the source moves toward the detector, so 𝑣<sub>s</sub> = + 22.0 m/s; the detector moves toward the source, so 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = −28.0 m/s.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>d</sub> ≈601 Hz

check.html: Both motions raise the pitch, and 601 Hz is above 520 Hz.

items.title: 4 (Lesson 1, Practice Problem 4): Whale-tracking ultrasound

body.html: A research boat emits ultrasound at 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 2.80 MHz while moving at 𝑣<sub>s</sub> = + 12.5 m/s toward a stationary detector in water. The speed of sound in water is 𝑣= 1497 m/s, and 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = 0. Find 𝑓<sub>d</sub>.
Moving source, stationary detector, with the speed of sound in water.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>d</sub> ≈2.82 MHz

check.html: The shift is small (about 0.8%) because 12.5 m/s is tiny compared with 1497 m/s.

items.title: 5 (Lesson 1, Practice Problem 5, Challenge): How fast must a train whistle move to raise an A to a B?

body.html: A whistle emits 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 440 Hz (A) and you want to hear 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 494 Hz (B), with 𝑣= 343 m/s and 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = 0. Find 𝑣<sub>s</sub> (moving toward the listener).
For a stationary detector, 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 𝑓<sub>s</sub> 𝑣/ (𝑣−𝑣<sub>s</sub>). Solve for 𝑣<sub>s</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑣<sub>s</sub> ≈37.5 m/s toward the listener (about 84 mph)

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) Problem 6: A speaker plays a steady tone. What should you change to make the sound higher in pitch? What should you change to make it quieter?

answer.html: Higher pitch: increase the frequency (equivalently, shorten the wavelength at fixed speed). Quieter: decrease the amplitude (the size of the pressure variation). The two changes are independent.

items.title: 7: Sketch the eardrum displacement versus time for 4.0 ms of a 0.50 kHz tone and of a 1.5 kHz tone.

body.html: The eardrum follows the pressure variation, so its displacement is a sine-like curve with the same period as the sound wave: 𝑇= 1 / 𝑓.

𝑇<sub>0.50</sub><sub> </sub><sub>kHz</sub> = 1 / 500 Hz = 2.0 ms, so 4.0 ms holds two cycles. 𝑇<sub>1.5</sub><sub> </sub><sub>kHz</sub> = 1 / 1500 Hz = 0.67 ms, so 4.0 ms holds six cycles. On the same time axis the 1.5 kHz curve has three times as many oscillations. Amplitudes are the same if the tones are equally loud.

answer.html: Two sine curves of equal amplitude: the 0.50 kHz tone has period 2.0 ms (two cycles in 4.0 ms); the 1.5 kHz tone has period 0.67 ms (six cycles in 4.0 ms), so its waves are three times as close together.

check.html: Tripling the frequency divides the period by three.

items.title: 8: A 600 Hz tone travels from air at 20°C into water at 25°C. Which of the speed, frequency, wavelength, and period change? Find the wavelengths.

body.html: 𝑓= 600 Hz, 𝑣<sub>air</sub> = 343 m/s, 𝑣<sub>water</sub> = 1497 m/s.
The medium sets the wave speed. The frequency is set by the source and stays the same across the boundary, so the period stays the same. The wavelength follows from 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓.

answer.html: The speed and wavelength change (wavelength goes from 0.572 m to 2.50 m, about 4.4 times longer). The frequency (600 Hz) and period do not change.

check.html: The wavelength ratio, 4.37, equals the speed ratio 1497 / 343, as it must when 𝑓 is fixed.

items.title: 9: How many times greater is the sound pressure level of a jet engine at close range (120 dB) than a whisper (40 dB)?

body.html: 120 dB and 40 dB; the book's rule is that 20 dB is a factor of 10.
The difference is 120 −40 = 80 dB.

answer.html: 10 000 times as great (pressure amplitude).

check.html: Four factors of 10 for four 20 dB steps.

items.title: 10: A worker taps one end of a long copper pipe and a friend puts an ear to the other end, 150 m away. Which sound arrives first, and by how much?

body.html: 𝑑= 150 m, 𝑣<sub>air</sub> = 343 m/s, 𝑣<sub>Cu</sub> = 4760 m/s (Table 1). Find both travel times.
Sound travels much faster in solids than in air, and the pipe guides the wave with little loss. 𝑡= 𝑑/ 𝑣.

answer.html: The sound through the copper arrives first, after 0.0315 s, versus 0.437 s through the air, which is about 0.41 s earlier (about 14 times sooner).

check.html: The time ratio, 0.437 / 0.0315 ≈13.9, equals the speed ratio 4760 / 343.

items.title: 11(a): A dolphin sends clicks at a large fish and at a small fish at the same distance. How do the two echoes compare?

answer.html: Both echoes have the same frequency and arrive after the same delay (same distance), but the larger fish reflects more of the sound, so its echo has a larger amplitude (is louder).

items.title: 11(b): How does the echo from a fish swimming toward the dolphin compare with the echo from one swimming away?

answer.html: From the fish swimming toward the dolphin, the echo has a higher frequency than the dolphin's click (Doppler shift up). From the fish swimming away, the echo has a lower frequency.

items.title: 12 (Critical Thinking): A speed camera uses radar from a post beside a straight road. Can it measure a motorcycle's speed at the instant the motorcycle is exactly level with the post?

body.html: The Doppler shift depends only on the component of the velocity along the line between the radar and the moving object.

When the motorcycle is level with the post, its velocity is perpendicular to the line joining them, so the component along that line is zero and the shift is zero. At an earlier moment, say when the line of sight makes 30° with the road, the radar sees only 𝑣cos30°. For a 25.0 m/s motorcycle that is (25.0 m/s)(cos30°) = 21.7 m/s.

answer.html: No. At the instant the motorcycle is level with the post its motion is perpendicular to the line of sight and gives no Doppler shift. The radar reads low (21.7 m/s instead of 25.0 m/s at 30°) unless it looks nearly along the road.

check.html: cos30° < 1 so any angled reading underestimates the true speed.

items.title: Encounter the Phenomenon: Why does a fire truck's siren change pitch as it passes you?

body.html: A siren emits a steady frequency 𝑓<sub>s</sub>. We need to explain why the heard pitch is higher on approach and lower on departure.

This is the Doppler effect. The wave speed in air depends only on the air, not on the source. When the source moves toward you, each new wave crest is emitted from a spot closer to you, so crests are bunched together (shorter wavelength). With the same wave speed, more crests arrive per second, so the frequency is higher.
Approaching: 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 𝑓<sub>s</sub>
<sup>𝑣</sup><sup>−</sup><sup>𝑣</sup><sub>s</sub> > 𝑓<sup>s</sup>. Receding: the source velocity is negative, so 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 𝑓<sub>s</sub>
<sup>𝑣</sup><sup>+</sup><sup> </sup><sup>|</sup><sup> 𝑣</sup><sub>s</sub><sup>|</sup> < 𝑓<sup>s</sup>. As the truck passes, the heard frequency drops from the high value to the low value.

answer.html: The truck moves toward you, then away. Approaching, the waves are compressed (shorter 𝜆 , higher 𝑓, higher pitch). Receding, they are stretched (longer 𝜆, lower 𝑓, lower pitch). The siren itself never changes its emitted frequency.

check.html: If the truck is at rest (𝑣<sub>s</sub> = 0) the formula gives 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 𝑓<sub>s</sub>, so there is no shift, as expected.

Use the Doppler effect results worked in this module. Evidence: Example Problem 1 and Practice Problem 1 (above): a 523 Hz source moving at 24.6 m/s is heard at about 564 Hz approaching (book) and 488 Hz receding. When 𝜆 is shortened, 𝑓= 𝑣/ 𝜆 rises; when 𝜆 is lengthened, 𝑓 falls. Pitch is determined by frequency, so you hear a higher pitch approaching and a lower pitch receding.

answer.html: The evidence supports the claim: relative motion of source and listener changes the frequency detected, so pitch changes while the siren's own frequency stays the same. (Wording of a CER is open-ended; the above is a model response.)

items.title: Focus Question: What factors affect the pitch of a sound?

answer.html: Pitch depends on the frequency of the sound wave (more vibrations per second means a higher pitch). Frequency can be changed by the source itself (for example, string tension or air- column length) or, as the Doppler effect shows, by relative motion between source and listener.

items.title: Get It? (page 362): Estimate the speed of sound in air at 25°C

body.html: 𝑣= 343 m/s at 20°C; speed rises about 0.6 m/s per 1°C. Find 𝑣 at 25°C.
Sound travels faster in warmer air; use the book's linear rule.
The temperature change is 25 −20 = 5°C.

check.html: Slightly larger than 343 m/s, as expected for warmer air.

items.title: Get It? (page 364): What characteristic of waves is pitch most closely linked to?

answer.html: Frequency. A higher frequency is heard as a higher pitch.

items.title: Get It? (page 364): How much more intense is an 80 dB sound than a 40 dB sound?

body.html: Sound levels of 80 dB and 40 dB. Find the ratio, using the book's rule that each 20 dB step is a factor of 10.
The decibel scale is logarithmic. The book says 20 dB means 10 times, 40 dB means 100 times (relative to the faintest sound).
The difference is 80 −40 = 40 dB, which is two steps of 20 dB.

answer.html: 100 times as great (in the book's convention, where 20 dB corresponds to a factor of 10). In the strict intensity-in-watts definition, a 40 dB difference would be a factor of 10<sup>4</sup> in intensity, which is 10<sup>2</sup> in pressure amplitude; the book's scale follows the pressure-amplitude version.

check.html: Higher dB means larger ratio, and 40 dB is a big gap, so a factor of 100 is sensible.

items.title: Figure 4 (Infer): About how many times louder does an alarm clock sound than heavy traffic?

body.html: From Figure 4, the alarm clock is at 80 dB and heavy traffic is at 70 dB. Find the loudness ratio.
The book states that most people perceive a 10 dB increase as about twice as loud.
80 −70 = 10 dB, which is one "doubling" of perceived loudness.

answer.html: About 2 times as loud.

check.html: The two levels are close on the scale, so a small multiple (2) is reasonable.

items.title: Figure 6 (Describe): What is the relative difference in the frequency of the detected sound for each observer?

body.html: Observer A is in front of the source, where waves are compressed; observer B is behind, where they are stretched.

answer.html: Observer A (source approaching) detects a higher frequency than the source emits, because 𝜆<sub>A</sub> is shorter. Observer B (source receding) detects a lower frequency, because 𝜆<sub>B</sub> is longer. So 𝑓<sub>A</sub> > 𝑓<sub>s</sub> > 𝑓<sub>B</sub>.

items.title: Get It? (page 366): Compare the wavelength and frequency heard by an observer in front of the moving fire engine with those heard behind it.

answer.html: In front of the fire engine the wavelength is shorter and the frequency is higher. Behind it the wavelength is longer and the frequency is lower. The product 𝑓𝜆= 𝑣 stays the same in both places because the speed of sound does not change.

items.title: Practice Problems (Doppler effect) Problem 1 (Lesson 1, Practice Problem 1): Repeat Example Problem 1 with the car moving away from you.

body.html: 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 523 Hz, 𝑣= 343 m/s, |𝑣<sub>s</sub> | = 24.6 m/s, 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = 0. Find 𝑓<sub>d</sub>.
Moving source, stationary detector. Positive direction is from source to detector, so a source moving away has 𝑣<sub>s</sub> = −24.6 m/s.

check.html: Lower than 523 Hz, as required for a receding source.

body.html: Figure 7 shows the car moving toward the siren at 25.0 m/s (labeled 𝑣<sub>d</sub>), 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 365 Hz, 𝑣= 343 m/s, source at rest (𝑣<sub>s</sub> = 0). Find 𝑓<sub>d</sub>.
Moving detector, stationary source. The positive axis points from source to detector, but the car moves toward the source, so 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = −25.0 m/s.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>d</sub> ≈392 Hz

check.html: Higher than 365 Hz, because you run into more crests each second.

body.html: Each car moves at 24.6 m/s toward the other. Horn 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 475 Hz, 𝑣= 343 m/s. Find the frequency you hear.
Both source and detector move. With the axis from source to detector: the source moves toward you, so 𝑣<sub>s</sub> = + 24.6 m/s; you move toward the source, so 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = −24.6 m/s.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>d</sub> ≈548 Hz

check.html: Both motions raise the pitch, and 548 Hz is above 475 Hz.

items.title: 4 (Lesson 1, Practice Problem 4): Submarine ultrasound

body.html: 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 3.50 MHz, 𝑣<sub>s</sub> = + 9.20 m/s (toward the detector), 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = 0, 𝑣= 1482 m/s. Find 𝑓<sub>d</sub>.
Moving source, stationary detector, with the speed of sound in water.

answer.html: 𝑓<sub>d</sub> ≈3.52 MHz

check.html: The shift is small (about 0.6%) because 9.2 m/s is tiny compared with 1482 m/s.

items.title: 5 (Lesson 1, Practice Problem 5, Challenge): How fast must a trumpet move to raise middle C to C sharp?

body.html: 𝑓<sub>s</sub> = 262 Hz, 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 277 Hz, 𝑣= 343 m/s, 𝑣<sub>d</sub> = 0. Find 𝑣<sub>s</sub> (moving toward the listener).
For a stationary detector, 𝑓<sub>d</sub> = 𝑓<sub>s</sub> 𝑣/ (𝑣−𝑣<sub>s</sub>). Solve for 𝑣<sub>s</sub>.

answer.html: 𝑣<sub>s</sub> ≈18.6 m/s toward the listener (about 42 mph)

check.html: 277/262 is about 1.057, so 𝑣<sub>s</sub> / 𝑣 should be about 5.4%; 18.6 / 343 = 0.054. Consistent.

items.title: Check Your Progress (Lesson 1) Problem 6: What physical characteristic of a sound wave should be changed to alter the pitch? The loudness?

answer.html: Pitch: change the frequency (or equivalently the wavelength, at fixed speed). Loudness: change the amplitude (the size of the pressure variation).

items.title: 7: Sketch the eardrum displacement versus time for two cycles of a 1.0 kHz tone and of a 2.0 kHz tone.

body.html: The eardrum follows the pressure variation, so its displacement is a sine-like curve with the same period as the sound wave: 𝑇= 1 / 𝑓.

𝑇<sub>1.0</sub><sub> </sub><sub>kHz</sub> = 1 / 1000 Hz = 1.0 ms, so two cycles last 2.0 ms. 𝑇<sub>2.0</sub><sub> </sub><sub>kHz</sub> = 0.50 ms, so two cycles last 1.0 ms. On the same time axis the 2.0 kHz curve has twice as many oscillations (four peaks in 2 ms versus two). Amplitudes are the same if the tones are equally loud.

answer.html: Two sine curves of equal amplitude: the 1.0 kHz tone has period 1.0 ms (two cycles over 2.0 ms); the 2.0 kHz tone has period 0.50 ms (two cycles over 1.0 ms), so its waves are twice as close together.

check.html: Doubling the frequency halves the period.

items.title: 8: List two characteristics of sound affected by the medium and two that are not.

body.html: The medium sets the wave speed. Wavelength follows from 𝜆= 𝑣/ 𝑓. The frequency is set by the source and does not change when the wave enters a new medium.

answer.html: Affected by the medium: the speed of sound and the wavelength (also how much it is absorbed). Not affected: the frequency (and therefore the pitch), which is set by the source. The sound's amplitude is determined by the source as well (although it fades with distance).

items.title: 9: How many times greater is the sound pressure level of a rock concert (110 dB) than a normal conversation (50 dB)?

body.html: 110 dB and 50 dB; the book's rule is that 20 dB is a factor of 10.
The difference is 110 −50 = 60 dB.

answer.html: 1000 times as great (pressure amplitude).

check.html: Three factors of 10 for three 20 dB steps. (In strict intensity terms, 60 dB would be 10<sup>6</sup> in intensity, which is 10<sup>3</sup> in pressure.)

items.title: 10: Why did putting an ear to a railroad track give early warning of an approaching train?

body.html: Sound travels much faster in solids than in air (Table 1: iron is about 4994 m/s, air about 343 m/s), and a steel rail guides the wave with little loss.
The speed ratio is about 4994 / 343 ≈15. The vibration from the train reaches you through the rail roughly 15 times sooner than the sound through air, and it is also louder.

answer.html: Sound moves through the steel rail about 15 times faster than through air and loses less energy, so the vibrations arrive well before the sound traveling through the air.

items.title: 11(a): Echoes from large and small insects at the same distance

answer.html: Both echoes have the same frequency and the same delay (same distance), but the larger insect reflects more of the sound, so its echo has a larger amplitude (is louder).

items.title: 11(b): Echo from an insect flying toward the bat versus away from it

answer.html: From an insect flying toward the bat, the echo has a higher frequency than the bat's pulse (Doppler shift up). From an insect flying away, the echo has a lower frequency.

items.title: 12 (Critical Thinking): Can a trooper at the side of the road measure a car's speed at the instant it passes?

body.html: The Doppler shift depends only on the component of the car's velocity along the line between the radar and the car.
When the car is directly beside the trooper, its velocity is perpendicular to that line, so the component along it is zero and the shift is zero.

answer.html: No. At the instant the car is exactly beside the trooper, its motion is perpendicular to the line of sight and gives no Doppler shift. The radar must measure the speed as the car approaches (or recedes), when the line of sight is nearly parallel to the road.
